title: Harnessing TLR4 Signaling Pathways in CAR Dendritic Cells to Overcome Tumor Immune Tolerance
text:
Solid tumors can be difficult to treat because they often avoid being attacked by the immune system. This
project will develop a new approach that uses specially engineered dendritic cells – which act like "generals" in
the immune system – to target and eliminate tumors as if they were an infection, with the goal of creating a
more effective and long-lasting cancer treatment.

title: Olfactory Phenotypes as Non-Invasive Biomarkers for Alzheimer's Disease: A Machine Learning Approach
text:
We predict that olfactory dysfunction testing using AROMA – a novel, essential oil-based, objective test of
olfaction – and machine learning algorithms using this data will accurately classify Alzheimer’s disease stage
(including asymptomatic individuals); be strongly associated with and predictive of conventional biomarkers of
disease; and predict longitudinal functional trajectory. The ability to effectively screen for ADRD using a non-
invasive and accessible test is critical to public health and our ability to identify people early when disease
course is most likely to still be modifiable. Accurate prediction of future functional decline will also meaningfully
inform comprehensive care planning and improved counseling of patients and their families.

title: Advanced Microscopy and Image Informatics
text: ADVANCED MICROSCOPY AND IMAGE INFORMATICS SHARED RESOURCE Imaging tools are critical to many aspects of the study of cancer biology, ranging from tissue and cellular level imaging with fluorescent microscopy platforms that offer routine-to-nanometer resolution of cellular structures to atomic resolution studies of specific macromolecules with specialized microscopy. The Advanced Microscopy and Image Informatics (AMII) Shared Resource (SR) provides high-quality microscopy and analytics services to the Dan L Duncan Comprehensive Cancer Center (DLDCCC) that spans multiple disciplines. The AMII SR is a resource for state-of-the-art imaging instrumentation, custom image analysis, and thorough one-on-one training by expert staff. Additional complimentary services are offered that include robust consultation for assay design and experimental setup, data acquisition on all available instruments, and image analysis approaches relevant to all acquired data using both custom-developed open source and commercial software platforms. The AMII SR Leaders and staff scientists are also heavily invested in education and training through graduate level teaching, hosting DLDCCC symposia, workshop and seminar organization, and one-on-one training of new (and current) users as needed by experts on staff. To ensure the best collection of data by DLDCCC faculty and/or trainees, the AMII SR also offers the option of utilizing its staff to perform wet-lab experiments from cell/tissue processing and labeling to fully assisted image acquisition across all platforms. Most notably, for fluorescence-based microscopy, the AMII SR offers deconvolution and confocal microscopy and assay development for high throughput imaging-based phenotypic or mechanistic screenings, including a halotomography platform for unlabeled phenotypic analysis of living cells. Further, the AMII SR has acquired numerous specialized small molecule libraries for high content screening, including collections relevant to known cancer-related and FDA-approved drugs, cancer metabolism, kinase and cell signaling inhibitors, nuclear receptor ligands, epigenetic and chromatin modifiers, lipid metabolism, endocrine disrupting chemicals. These small molecules and genomic perturbations are all amenable to single cell-oriented Cell Painting-based screening with a novel, custom-built open-source software platform now in regular use. New for this renewal, cryo electron microscopy (CryoEM), and cellular cryo electron tomography (CryoET) with cryo focused ion beam milling (CryoFIB) services have been added. The addition of CryoEM services permit submicron milling of tissues and cellular specimens with subsequent 3-D imaging at 5 nm resolution. Additionally, CryoEM services permit structural studies of purified molecules and macromolecular assemblies to near atomic resolution. Previously, as a stand-alone College resource, the well-established set of CryoEM/ET services have already been heavily used by dozens of cancer researchers for diverse purposes, from studying the high-resolution structure of nuclear hormone receptors to studying the internal structure of exosomes and circulating tumor cells. Incorporation into AMII will enhance access to these methods and provide opportunities for improved outreach and education.

title: Discovery of efflux pump inhibitors using a high-throughout bacterial assay
text:
Antibiotic resistance is a worldwide problem that will continue to present challenges to the healthcare industry.
Bacteria possess several mechanisms of antibiotic resistance, including target mutations, degradation
mechanisms, reduced permeability, and the presence of efflux pumps. The goal of this project is to develop a
high-throughput assay to identify inhibitors of efflux pumps, which confer bacteria a key mechanism to evade
antibiotics.

title: Core 1
text:
The Data Collection and Clinical Genetics Core serves as a hub in support of data and biospecimen collection 
across multiple projects aimed at understanding the role of inherited susceptibility to cancer in African Americans 
and improving access to genetic counseling and testing services in this population. It also extends participation 
in research by providing clinical genetic testing based on research findings.

title: Core C: Bioinformatics and Genomics Core
text: Project Summary/Abstract – Core C Bioinformatics has become an integral part of biological research due to the high-throughput nature of multi-omics experiments warranting the need for having the infrastructure and trained personnel to support the advancement of science of the research projects. The Bioinformatics and Genomics Core (Core C) will continue to serve as a linchpin in the overall success of the program project by supporting the generation, storage, processing, analysis and accessing of experimental data. Core C will be led by Drs. Babu Guda and James Eudy, who will provide complementary expertise in Bioinformatics and Genomics areas, respectively. This Core is innovative by having a fully integrated Bioinformatics as well as Genomics units within, which allows full spectrum access to cutting-edge experimental and analytical techniques under one Core. The specific aims are: Aim 1: Support the sequencing and analysis of multi-omics data for research projects. Aim 2: Integrative analysis and functional characterization of significant genes, gene products, enriched pathways, and upstream regulators for hypothesis generation and testing. Aim 3: Develop a web portal to centralize access to multi-omics data from all research projects and to facilitate bioinformatics training activities. Core C will make a big impact on the overall success of the project by providing resources, personnel support and developing cutting-edge technologies and custom data analysis methods for all research projects. Proposed cloud-based web portal backed by a searchable database provides easy access to all experimental data, metadata, and the training materials facilitating synergistic interactions among the project personnel across multiple sites.

title: Cartilage targeting exosomes for OA gene therapy and pain treatment
text:
Cartilage repair remains a challenge due to its avascular and negatively charged matrix that limits its regenerative
ability and hinders drug transport, which already suffer from short joint residence time. Mesenchymal stem cell
derived exosomes are emerging as promising cartilage repair therapy due to their intrinsic regenerative potential,
but they suffer from lack of cartilage targeting. This project will make them positively charged such that they can
penetrate the negatively charged cartilage, use it as a drug depot and deliver the packed gene therapeutics while
also exhibiting their natural pro-chondrogenic potential to both repair cartilage and provide pain relief.

title: Advanced Technology Core
text: ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY CORE (CORE C) PROJECT SUMMARY Leveraging the collective scientific expertise and resources across the DC CFAR partner institutions, the Advanced Technology Core (ATC) will provide an array of high impact laboratory services and training to HIV investigators in Washington, DC. Under the leadership of NIH-funded senior scientists and with a cadre of DC CFAR-supported Core service providers, the ATC will actively support high priority advanced technology services in virology, immunology, proteomics and bioinformatics, and provide access to other key laboratory services that utilize advanced technologies including single-cell analysis, -omics, specialized immunologic assays, CRISPR technologies, complex imaging, cryo-electron microscopy, machine learning, and HIV reservoir assays. The ATC will assist investigators in acquiring preliminary data for grant applications; conduct funded research protocols; and foster linkages with the Scientific Working Groups (SWGs) and Scientific Interest Groups (SIGs) and clinical and translational investigators. For Specific Aim 1, the ATC will provide high impact and advanced technology laboratory services (including single-cell analysis, omics, specialized immunology, CRISPR technologies, complex imaging, cryo-electron microscopy, machine learning, and HIV reservoir assays) to DC CFAR investigators. For Specific Aim 2, the ATC will facilitate service dissemination and training in advanced techniques and assays to recipients of Pilot, Transitioning Investigator, and NIH awards by organizing DC CFAR institutional workshops, the Core service laboratory “open house” series, and the annual Core Service Providers Research Day. For Specific Aim 3, the ATC will promote multidisciplinary forums by organizing workshops and seminars with the goal of connecting social, behavioral, clinical, and population scientists with the basic science investigators who are utilizing advanced technologies. These activities will contribute to addressing the DC CFAR mission of ending the HIV epidemic in Washington, DC and improving the health and quality of life of persons with HIV.

title: Mechanisms of RHOA signaling in regulating vascular integrity and development
text:
RHOA signaling is implicated in cranial vascular disease states with impaired blood vessel integrity, including
hemorrhagic stroke and cerebral cavernous malformations. Through combined molecular and genetic studies
conducted in vivo in zebrafish and in vitro in human endothelial cells, this research plan aims to elucidate the
roles that RHOA and its effectors ROCK1, ROCK2, and others play in regulating cranial vascular integrity and
development. By defining and characterizing members of the endothelial cell-specific RHOA signaling network,
we will better understand how RHOA and its effectors participate in normal vascular development and disease.

title: Developing a PET tracer targeting myeloperoxidase activity for neurodegenerative diseases
text:
Myeloperoxidase is a key damaging enzyme secreted in many neurodegenerative diseases, including
Alzheimer's disease. The goal of this proposal is to develop and characterize a new PET imaging agent to
specifically and sensitively map myeloperoxidase activity in the brain, validate this agent in a mouse model of
Alzheimer's disease, and prepare for regulatory filing.

title: The role of genome folding in regulating gene expression and chromatin state
text:
The goal of this project is to elucidate fundamental knowledge of the link between three-dimensional genome
organization and gene expression. This research will investigate the properties of cohesin complexes, identify
and characterize novel cohesin-interacting proteins, and elucidate the role of cohesin-mediated DNA loops in
regulation of transcription and chromatin state. This knowledge is critical for understanding human health and
disease states linked to altered three-dimensional genome organization, such as developmental disorders and
cancers.

title: RDCD Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT, RDCD CORE Quality clinical and translational research is impossible without strong support for research design and compliance. To this end, the overarching goal of the Research Design, Compliance, and Data Management (RDCD) Core is to provide accessible, rigorous research design, analytic, and data support services, and compliance support for the partner institutions of the Mississippi Center for Clinical and Translational Research (MCCTR). The RDCD Core is the central resource for high-level expertise in research design, epidemiology, biostatistics, bioinformatics, AI, and regulatory compliance. The MCCTR aims to facilitate clinical, translational, and population health research on chronic diseases affecting Mississippians. The MCCTR’s strong record in research in diabetes, CKD, hypertension, imaging of disease, heart disease, cancer, and maternal/fetal disorders will be further strengthened and expanded into other chronic disease domains moving forward with the ultimate goal of improving the health of Mississippians. The RDCD Core will play a pivotal role. Studies that are appropriately powered, well-designed, with rigorous analytics, and that meet all regulatory standards are critical to accomplishing these goals. The Core will also lead into new frontiers with the emerging and transformative fields of bioinformatics and AI. During Phase III, we will expand support for the clinical and translational research spectrum from bench science to randomized trials to community-engaged research, including support for initial study design, federal and institutional regulatory compliance, biostatistical/bioinformatics analysis, and risk and safety. In collaboration with the UMMC Office of the Associate Vice Chancellor for Research, we will continue to expand access to current data resources, provide regulatory and compliance support, and provide directed training on matters related to Core functions through the following specific aims: (Aim 1) Support and train MCCTR investigators and users on research design, biostatistical analysis, risk assessment, safety protocols, and deep learning and artificial intelligence models, (Aim 2) Leverage existing infrastructure to provide support for dataset curation and management while ensuring validation and minimizing bias; and (Aim 3) Through the Compliance Sub-core, provide investigators the necessary tools and expertise to ensure adherence to all regulatory and compliance standards at the institutional, state, and federal levels. The RDCD Core is committed to outstanding support for the growing clinical, translational, and population research infrastructure, which will play a critical role in alleviating the burden of major chronic diseases impacting Mississippians.

title: Understanding expression and signaling of sex hormone receptors in brain cancers
text: IDH-mutant gliomas are universally lethal primary brain tumors driven by profound metabolic reprogramming, yet key aspects of their altered metabolism remain poorly understood. This project investigates a newly discovered metabolic feature of these tumors—accumulation of the metabolite itaconate—to determine how it is produced and how it influences tumor growth, metabolism, immune interactions, and response to therapy.  Understanding this pathway may reveal new targets for improving treatment outcomes in patients with IDHmutant glioma.

title: Examining the role of novel proenkephalin peptides in influencing alcohol-induced cognitive dysfunction
text:
Alcohol consumption stimulates the release of endogenously-produced opioid peptides that influence the
rewarding effects of this drug. With continued consumption and over time, the ability to stimulate the same level
of response changes fundamentally, although it is not known if such changes include the production of novel
peptides from the same family. Here we will apply the use of advanced analytical platforms and animal models
of addiction towards the study of a novel peptide that we believe may be influencing cognitive impairments in
individuals with Alcohol Use Disorder.

title: Role of FABP7 in ALS models
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or Lou Gehrig’s disease is characterized by the specific death of the nerve
cells that control muscle movement, leading to paralysis and eventual death. ALS is linked to inflammation and
defects in energy metabolism. This proposal will investigate if altered expression of a protein that binds fatty
acids and regulates inflammation and metabolism plays a role in the progression of the disease in ALS-models.

title: Deciphering Human-KSHV Protein Interactions Driving Kaposi Sarcoma with AI Models
text:
This project aims to develop an AI-driven framework to identify and validate KSHV-host protein-protein
interactions that suppress the cGAS-STING pathway, revealing novel mechanisms of immune evasion and
providing new targets for the treatment of Kaposi Sarcoma.

title: The Use of Chest Radiography in Detecting Early TB in Children and Youth
text:
It is now widely accepted that after the establishment of TB infection, it may progress and regress across
several subclinical states for a wide range of durations — from weeks to several years — before emerging as
active TB disease. Emerging evidence indicates that infectiousness can precede the classic symptoms of
active TB disease, so individuals in these subclinical stages of TB are often overlooked in TB control programs,
including active TB case-finding programs. Our proposal aims to evaluate the use of chest radiography to
identify individuals in these subclinical stages, enabling timely non-therapeutic or therapeutic interventions to
help interrupt further transmission of TB.

title: Role of C difficile Colonization in Risk of Disease
text:
Clostridioides difficile infection remains one of the most common healthcare-associated infections. While C.
difficile carriage is both highly prevalent and strongly associated with risk of subsequent disease, factors that
prevent or promote progression to disease remain poorly understood. The proposed work will apply bioinformatic
methods to a well-characterized biorepository of carriers to advance the current understanding of progression
from C. difficile carriage to disease, with the ultimate goal of informing future prevention efforts.

title: Neuronal Primary Cilia Dysfunction in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex
text:
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disorder with high rates of epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder,
and intellectual disability, but the cellular mechanisms underlying these neurological symptoms are not well
understood. We have found that the primary cilium, a sensory organelle, is altered in neurons of TSC patients.
In this study, we will investigate the molecular mechanism underlying this alteration and its functional
implications.

title: Uncovering the unique roles of bone-forming osteoblasts and bone endothelial cells in organ-specific metastasis of breast cancer to bone
text:
My proposed research aims to develop cost-effective, user-friendly, and high-throughput microfluidic cancer
metastasis models, leveraging organ-on-a-chip (OoC) technology, to advance our understanding of the complex
mechanisms underlying breast cancer's (BC) predilection for bone metastasis. I will create BC metastasis models
that will elucidate the specific roles of osteoblasts, bone endothelial cells, and BC cells in the critical processes
of BC bone extravasation and early colonization. This research has the potential to uncover new insights into
BC bone metastasis and to lead to innovative therapeutic interventions, which directly aligns with the mission of
the National Cancer Institute (NCI).
